title: How do you perform a Root Cause Analysis (RCA) and write a blameless post-mortem after a production incident?
shortTitle: Performing a Root Cause Analysis (RCA) and writing a blameless post-mortem after a production incident

s1_definition.profdef: Root Cause Analysis is the disciplined investigation that works backward from an incident's symptoms through the chain of contributing factors to the underlying systemic causes, rather than stopping at the first trigger. A blameless post-mortem is the written record of an incident that focuses on how the system and processes allowed the failure, deliberately avoiding naming individuals as at fault, so that engineers feel safe telling the full truth. Together they produce concrete, owned, tracked action items that make the same class of failure less likely, because the goal is organizational learning, not punishment.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose the National Bank of India accidentally double-charged a batch of transfers one night. A blameful approach asks "who pressed the wrong button" and fires them, which teaches everyone else to hide mistakes. The blameless approach asks "how was it even possible for one button press to double-charge customers like Rajesh and Priya, and why did nothing catch it before it reached production?" It traces the failure back: the engineer followed the documented procedure, but the procedure was wrong, the test environment did not match production, and there was no safety check on duplicate charges. The fix is not punishing a person; it is fixing the procedure, the test environment, and adding the safety check — so no future engineer can cause the same harm.
s1_definition.oneliner: RCA traces an incident back to systemic causes, and a blameless post-mortem records it focusing on the system not the person, producing tracked fixes so the same failure cannot recur.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Root Cause Analysis is the disciplined investigation that works backward from an incident's symptoms through the chain of contributing factors to the underlying systemic causes, rather than stopping at the first trigger. A blameless post-mortem is the written record of an incident that focuses on how the system and processes allowed the failure, deliberately avoiding naming individuals as at fault, so that engineers feel safe telling the full truth. Together they produce concrete, owned, tracked action items that make the same class of failure less likely, because the goal is organizational learning, not punishment.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose the National Bank of India accidentally double-charged a batch of transfers one night. A blameful approach asks "who pressed the wrong button" and fires them, which teaches everyone else to hide mistakes. The blameless approach asks "how was it even possible for one button press to double-charge customers like Rajesh and Priya, and why did nothing catch it before it reached production?" It traces the failure back: the engineer followed the documented procedure, but the procedure was wrong, the test environment did not match production, and there was no safety check on duplicate charges. The fix is not punishing a person; it is fixing the procedure, the test environment, and adding the safety check — so no future engineer can cause the same harm.

**One line to remember:** RCA traces an incident back to systemic causes, and a blameless post-mortem records it focusing on the system not the person, producing tracked fixes so the same failure cannot recur.

sections.s2_technical:
An incident response has phases, and RCA begins once the immediate fire is out. First you detect and mitigate — stop the bleeding, restore service, often by rolling back or failing over, before you fully understand the cause. Then you assemble a factual timeline: exactly when the change went out, when the first alert fired, when a human noticed, what actions were taken and when, and when service recovered. The timeline is built from hard evidence — logs, metrics, deploy records, chat transcripts — not memory, because memory is unreliable under stress.

The core of RCA is refusing to stop at the trigger. The trigger is the proximate event, like "a bad config was deployed," but the root cause is why that was possible and why it was not caught. A widely used technique is the Five Whys: you ask why repeatedly, each answer exposing a deeper layer. The config was bad — why? Because a value was typed wrong — why did that reach production? Because the config had no validation — why not? Because the deploy pipeline did not lint configs — why not? Because we never prioritised it. Each why moves from the person toward the system. A good RCA usually finds several contributing causes, not one, because real incidents are the result of multiple missing safeguards lining up — the layers of a system each had a hole, and the holes aligned. You also distinguish the root cause from aggravating factors that made the incident worse or longer, such as a slow alert or a confusing dashboard.

A blameless post-mortem is the written artifact, and blamelessness is a specific, deliberate discipline, not vagueness. It assumes every person acted reasonably with the information and tools they had at the time, so when someone made a mistake, the real question is what about the system made that mistake easy or likely. You write "the engineer ran the documented rollback command, which unexpectedly also cleared the cache" rather than "the engineer carelessly cleared the cache." This matters practically: if people fear blame, they hide details, and you lose the information needed to actually fix the system. Blamelessness is what makes the truth come out.

The post-mortem has a standard structure: a short summary, the impact quantified in real terms (how many customers, how much money, how long), the timeline, the root cause and contributing factors, what went well and what went poorly in the response, and the action items. The action items are the whole point — each must be specific, assigned to an owner, tracked in the backlog with a due date, and prioritised, otherwise the post-mortem is theatre. You distinguish detection improvements (catch it faster next time), prevention (stop it happening), and mitigation (limit the damage). A senior nuance: you run post-mortems for near-misses too, not just customer-facing outages, because a near-miss is a free lesson. You hold a post-mortem review meeting where the document is discussed openly, you share it widely so other teams learn, and you measure whether action items actually get completed, because the sign of a mature organization is not having zero incidents but learning permanently from each one.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India's transfer service had a thirty-minute outage: a bad configuration deploy caused transfers to fail for Rajesh, Priya, and thousands of others. The team must perform an RCA and produce a blameless post-mortem with tracked action items.

Problem 1 — The team must build a factual timeline from evidence: when the deploy happened, when the alert fired, when a human responded, when it was mitigated by rollback, and when service fully recovered, to compute the real impact.

Problem 2 — The team must run the Five Whys to move from the trigger (bad config) to the systemic root causes (no config validation, no staging parity, slow alerting), identifying multiple contributing factors rather than one scapegoat.

Problem 3 — The team must generate specific, owned, tracked action items categorised as detection, prevention, and mitigation, phrased blamelessly.

Our runnable Java simulation models a `Postmortem` that holds a timeline of `TimelineEvent`s and computes impact, a `FiveWhys` chain that drills from symptom to root cause, and an `ActionItem` list with owners and categories, with a `PostmortemDemo` main that assembles and prints the full blameless report. Classes: `TimelineEvent`, `FiveWhys`, `ActionItem`, `Postmortem`, and the demo.

##### 4c. Configuration File — the written post-mortem template

```markdown
<!-- postmortems/2026-10-29-transfer-outage.md -->
# Post-Mortem: Transfer Service Outage (2026-10-29)  [BLAMELESS]

## Summary
A configuration deploy at 14:02 caused all transfers to fail for 30 minutes.

## Impact
- ~12,400 failed transfers (incl. Rajesh SAV2001, Priya CUR3001)
- ~Rs.6.2 crore in delayed transfer volume
- Duration: 14:02 -> 14:32 (30 min)

## Root Cause (and contributing factors)
Trigger: an invalid `pool.maxSize=0` value shipped in a config deploy.
Root causes (systemic):
  1. No config validation in the deploy pipeline (prevention gap)
  2. Staging did not mirror prod config (detection gap)
  3. Alert fired after 8 min, not immediately (detection gap)

## What went well / poorly
- Well: rollback was fast once identified (4 min)
- Poorly: no automated config lint; staging parity missing

## Action Items (owned, tracked)
- [ ] (PREVENT) add config schema validation to pipeline — @platform — due 11-05
- [ ] (DETECT)  staging config parity check — @sre — due 11-12
- [ ] (DETECT)  alert on transfer error-rate within 1 min — @sre — due 11-08
- [ ] (MITIGATE) canary config rollout (1% first) — @platform — due 11-20
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the facts of a thirty-minute transfer outage — a config deploy at 14:02, failures beginning immediately, an alert at 14:10, root cause identified at 14:28, and recovery at 14:32 — plus twelve thousand four hundred affected transfers.

Step 1: The post-mortem assembles the factual timeline from evidence, placing each event at its real time. From the first and last events it computes the outage duration of thirty minutes, and with the affected-transfer count it quantifies the impact in concrete terms.

Step 2: The Five Whys analysis starts from the symptom that all transfers failed and drills down. The first why finds the connection pool had a size of zero; the next finds a bad config value was deployed; the next finds the pipeline did not validate config; the next finds validation was never added; the final why reaches the systemic gap that there was no guardrail requiring config schema checks. The chain deliberately moves from the event toward the system.

Step 3: The identified root cause is systemic, not a person. The analysis explicitly frames it as a system gap, which is what keeps the post-mortem blameless — the engineer who deployed followed the normal process, and the process lacked a safety net.

Step 4: Action items are generated across all three categories: prevention adds config validation, detection adds staging parity and a faster alert, and mitigation adds a canary rollout. Each item has an owner and a due date so it is tracked rather than forgotten.

Step 5: The post-mortem is published with impact, timeline, root cause, and owned action items, closing with the reminder that the purpose is to fix the system, not punish a person. The output is a learning artifact the whole organization can read.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Root Cause Analysis is the disciplined investigation that works backward from an incident's symptoms through the chain of contributing factors to the underlying systemic causes, and a blameless post-mortem is the written record that focuses on how the system allowed the failure rather than who caused it. I always separate the phases: first detect and mitigate to stop the bleeding, usually by rolling back or failing over before I fully understand the cause, then build a factual timeline from hard evidence — deploy logs, metrics, chat transcripts — not from memory, because memory is unreliable under stress.

The heart of RCA is refusing to stop at the trigger. The trigger is the proximate event, like a bad config deploy, but the root cause is why that was even possible and why nothing caught it. I use the Five Whys, asking why repeatedly so each answer exposes a deeper layer and moves from the person toward the system, and I expect to find several contributing causes rather than one, because real incidents happen when multiple missing safeguards line up. Blamelessness is a specific discipline, not vagueness: I assume everyone acted reasonably with the information and tools they had, so when someone made a mistake the real question is what about the system made that mistake easy. This matters practically, because if people fear blame they hide details and I lose the very information I need to fix the system.

The post-mortem itself has a standard shape — a summary, quantified impact, the timeline, the root cause and contributing factors, what went well and poorly, and above all the action items. The action items are the entire point: each must be specific, assigned to an owner, tracked in the backlog with a due date, and categorised as detection, prevention, or mitigation, or the post-mortem is just theatre. In my project at the National Bank of India, a config deploy with a connection pool size of zero took down transfers for twelve thousand customers including Rajesh and Priya for thirty minutes. The Five Whys took us from the failed transfers down to the systemic gap that the deploy pipeline had no config validation, and we came out with owned, dated action items — config schema validation to prevent, staging parity and a faster alert to detect, and a canary rollout to mitigate. We shared it org-wide and tracked the items to completion. The principle I always state is that the measure of a mature organization is not having zero incidents but learning permanently from every one, and that only happens when people feel safe enough to tell the whole truth.
